What the official sources say

  • Written abatement application to the assessors must be filed within 185 days from commitment; assessors may also abate on their own initiative within one year. (36 M.R.S. §841(1); source)
  • After one year but within 3 years from commitment, the municipal officers may abate for illegality, error or irregularity, but may not grant an abatement to correct an error in valuation. (36 M.R.S. §841(1); source)
  • If a municipality has a board of assessment review, an applicant denied abatement may appeal in writing to it within 60 days after notice of the decision or deemed denial. (36 M.R.S. §843(1); source)
  • Residential appeals from the board of assessment review go directly to Superior Court under Rule 80B; nonresidential property or property with equalized municipal valuation of $1,000,000 or greater goes to the State Board of Property Tax Review within 60 days. (36 M.R.S. §843(1), (1-A); source)
  • A taxpayer filing an appeal must pay the greater of the prior year's taxes (up to current taxes due) or the undisputed current taxes; this does not apply to property valued under $500,000. (36 M.R.S. §843(4); source)
  • 'Certified ratio' is the level of assessed value, as a percentage of just value, as certified by the assessor under 36 M.R.S. §383. (Maine Revenue Services Property Tax Bulletin 31; source)
  • Maine uses a tax lien mortgage rather than a tax sale: if unpaid within 18 months after filing the certificate, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and redemption expires. (36 M.R.S. §943; source)

How does Maine property tax work?

Maine property tax is set and collected by each municipality, and it is based on what you own on April 1. 36 M.R.S. §502 fixes the status of taxpayers and taxable property as of April 1, and the taxable year runs April 1 to March 31.

Each town sets its own due dates and interest. Under §505 a municipality votes the date or dates taxes are due, the date interest begins (which is also the delinquency date), and the rate. The rate cannot exceed the prime rate plus 3 percentage points as set by the Treasurer of State, and the state posts the maximum by January 20 each year. Towns may allow an early-payment discount of up to 10%.

Because of this, a Maine seller needs to read the town's own bill. Two houses of the same value in neighboring towns can have different due dates, different rates and different ratios.

What does the statewide picture look like?

Maine Revenue Services publishes a yearly Municipal Valuation Return summary. The 2025 report shows a total commitment of $3,650,756,363 on total taxable municipal valuation of $284,892,094,527. In the 2024 report, Cumberland County had the largest valuation at about $70.7 billion, or roughly 28% of the state total, followed by York County at about $53.9 billion. Portland had the largest single municipal valuation at about $14.8 billion.

MeasureFigureYear
Total commitment$3,650,756,3632025
Total taxable municipal valuation$284,892,094,5272025
Homestead exemptions325,426 totaling $7,410,258,9602025
Cumberland County valuationAbout $70.7 billion2024
Range of municipal certified ratios50% to 112%2024

The certified ratio is the level of assessed value as a percentage of just value, as certified by the assessor under 36 M.R.S. §383 (Property Tax Bulletin 31). A town at 80% assesses at four-fifths of market value, which is one reason you cannot compare bills across towns without comparing the ratio and the rate.

How do you challenge a Maine property tax assessment?

You file a written abatement application with the assessors within 185 days of commitment. 36 M.R.S. §841 lets assessors abate for illegality, error or irregularity on an application within that period, or on their own initiative within one year. After one year and up to three years, the municipal officers may act, but they may not abate to correct a valuation error.

Maine Revenue Services Bulletin No. 10 explains the practice:

  • Ask for your property record card and check it for errors such as the wrong build year or acreage.
  • The request must state the amount and the reason, and you carry the burden of proof. Disagreeing with the value is not enough.
  • Useful evidence includes factual mistakes on the card, recent sales of comparable local properties and neighborhood sales data.
  • If the assessor mailed a request for property information under §706-A, answer it, or you may lose the right to appeal.
  • The assessors must decide within 60 days. No written decision in that time means the request is deemed denied.

Taxes are still due on the normal dates while an abatement is pending, according to the Cumberland County assessing page. That page also says the assessment is presumed valid and cites 36 M.R.S. §848-A, under which an assessment is defended if it is accurate within reasonable limits unless a deviation of 10% or more is proven.

Where does an appeal go after the abatement is denied?

After a denial, a taxpayer has 60 days to appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review. Section 843 says that if the board does not issue a written decision within 60 days, the application is deemed denied unless the applicant agrees in writing to a delay.

LevelWhoDeadline or rule
Abatement applicationAssessors185 days from commitment
Board of Assessment ReviewLocal board60 days after notice or deemed denial
Superior CourtResidential property, Rule 80BDirect appeal from the board; Bulletin 10 gives 30 days
State Board of Property Tax ReviewNonresidential property or $1,000,000 or more60 days from the board decision

Where no local board exists, Bulletin 10 says the first appeal goes to the county commissioners. Residential property appeals go from the board directly to Superior Court. A taxpayer on property valued at $500,000 or more must pay the greater of the prior year's taxes (up to current taxes) or the undisputed current taxes while the appeal runs, and the appeal is suspended if the taxpayer does not.

What happens if you fall behind on Maine property tax?

Maine uses a tax lien mortgage, not a tax sale. The collector may send a demand notice after 8 months and within one year of commitment, giving 30 days to pay, then records a tax lien certificate at the registry of deeds within 10 days after that period ends (36 M.R.S. §942).

Under §943 the recorded certificate creates a tax lien mortgage that ranks ahead of other liens. If the debt remains unpaid 18 months after recording, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and the right of redemption ends. The treasurer must notify the owner and mortgage holders 30 to 45 days before the foreclosure date.

  • Owners claiming the homestead exemption must receive notice of the hardship abatement process and sources of foreclosure-avoidance help.
  • The taxpayer pays recording and discharge fees plus $13 and any foreclosure notice charge.
  • If the taxpayer dies with a probated will, a probate judge may allow up to 60 more days to redeem.
  • After foreclosure the town holds title and can sell the property.

For an owner in this position, the clock is the 18 months. A sale that closes before then pays the town from proceeds and ends the problem.

Is there hardship relief on a Maine tax bill?

Yes. Under §841(2), municipal officers can abate taxes on a primary residence for a person unable to pay because of hardship or poverty, within three years of commitment. The officers must give a written decision within 30 days of the application, and the proceedings are confidential.

Maine also runs a State Property Tax Deferral Program. You must be 65 or older or unable to work from permanent disability, own a primary residence, have household income under $80,000, and have liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with more than one owner). The state pays the town, then places a lien on the home. Selling the home triggers repayment of the deferred taxes, interest and costs. A new municipal lien prevents future deferral.

The Maine homestead exemption lowers the taxable value by up to $25,000 for a permanent resident, adjusted by the local certified ratio.

How is property tax handled at a Maine closing?

Buyer and seller can agree to split the year's tax on a pro rata basis. 36 M.R.S. §558 says taxes are prorated over the municipality's fiscal year unless the parties agree to a different period.

Remember that the town assesses to whoever owned the property on April 1. If a sale changes the owner, §502 lets the assessor update the records after a declaration of value is filed, and notice of the tax goes to both the new owner and the April 1 owner of record.

The transfer tax is separate. The state charges $2.20 per $500 of value, divided evenly between buyer and seller under §4641-A. Over $1,000,000 an extra $3.80 per $500 applies to the excess.

What should a Maine seller with tax due do first?

  1. Call the town tax collector for a payoff figure, including interest and any lien charges.
  2. Check whether a lien certificate has been recorded at the county registry of deeds, and count the months from the recording date.
  3. Ask the assessor for the property record card and compare it against the house.
  4. Note the abatement dates. The 185-day window runs from commitment, which is about when bills first go out.
  5. Tell any buyer about deferral liens, since the state must be repaid at transfer.

If the taxes, a lien and needed repairs all sit on the same house, a cash sale can close without waiting on a buyer's lender, and the tax payoff comes from proceeds. Cash Home Buyers buys Maine houses as-is, and we do not set a price until we have looked at the property.

More questions about Maine Property Tax Guide

When is Maine property tax assessed?

As of April 1. Under 36 M.R.S. §502, what you own on April 1 fixes who is taxed for that year, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31.

How long do I have to apply for a property tax abatement in Maine?

185 days from the date of commitment. Assessors may also abate on their own within one year, and municipal officers may act on certain errors for up to three years.

Can I appeal an assessor's denial?

Yes. File in writing with the local Board of Assessment Review within 60 days of the decision or deemed denial. Residential cases then go to Superior Court under Rule 80B.

Does Maine have tax sales?

No. Maine uses a tax lien mortgage. If it stays unpaid 18 months after the lien certificate is recorded, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and redemption ends.

Who pays Maine's real estate transfer tax?

Buyer and seller each pay half, at $2.20 per $500 of value, with an added $3.80 per $500 above $1,000,000.

What happens to a deferred tax balance when I sell?

Selling or transferring the home requires repayment of all deferred taxes, interest and costs to the state.

Do I have to pay taxes while an appeal is pending?

Taxes stay due on the normal dates. For property valued at $500,000 or more, you must pay the greater of last year's taxes or the undisputed current taxes.

What the official sources say

  • The homestead exemption reduces the value of a home for property tax purposes by up to $25,000. (Homestead Exemption Program FAQ | Maine Revenue Services; source)
  • Qualifying requires Maine permanent residency, the home as permanent residence, 12 months of Maine homestead ownership, and an application filed with the municipality on or before April 1. (Homestead Exemption Program FAQ | Maine Revenue Services; source)
  • The statute exempts $10,000 of just value under subsection 1 plus an additional $15,000 for tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2020. (36 M.R.S. §683(1), (1-B); source)
  • Section 683 states the exemptions are discontinued beginning with property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2027. (36 M.R.S. §683(6); source)
  • A permanent resident who loses a homestead to tax lien foreclosure and regains it from the municipality is deemed to have continuously owned it. (36 M.R.S. §683(1); source)

What is the Maine homestead exemption and how much does it take off?

The Maine homestead exemption lowers the taxable value of your permanent home by up to $25,000. The Maine Revenue Services program FAQ says the amount is adjusted by the local certified ratio, so a town with an 80% ratio gives an exemption of $20,000. The exemption cannot be larger than the value of the homestead itself.

Under 36 M.R.S. §683 the $25,000 is built from two pieces: $10,000 of just value in the base subsection, plus an additional $15,000 for tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2020. It sits on top of other exemptions that a homeowner may already hold, such as the ones in sections 653 and 654-A. It is not a credit on the bill. It shrinks the value the town multiplies by its tax rate.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. The exemption is attached to a person who lives in the house, not to the house forever. When ownership or residence changes, the break stops, and the next owner has to qualify on their own.

Who qualifies for the Maine homestead exemption?

You qualify if you are a permanent Maine resident, the home is your permanent residence, and you have owned a home in Maine for the twelve months before you apply. Those three tests come from the Maine Revenue Services Homestead Exemption Program FAQ and from the statute.

  • Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not count. You can have only one permanent residence at a time.
  • The home must be residential property assessed as real property. A mobile home on a rented lot may qualify.
  • Permanent residence is presumed to continue until circumstances show otherwise. The test is whether you intend to return when you are away.
  • There is no income limit. A task force report covered by the press notes that the exemption is open to permanent-resident homeowners, not renters.
  • If the home has several owners, only one signature is required on the application. The exemption can be divided among co-owners who live there in proportion to their interests.

A person who loses a homestead to tax lien foreclosure and later gets it back from the municipality is treated as having owned it the whole time, and the town's brief ownership does not disqualify them.

How and when do you file for the exemption in Maine?

You file a written application with your municipal assessor on or before April 1. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment, so a late application costs a full tax year of savings.

Most towns hand out the form, and Maine Revenue Services also posts it on its property tax forms page. The program FAQ gives two answers about where to file: one says the municipality where the property is located and another says the municipality where you reside. For a normal owner-occupied house those are the same town, so call the assessor if yours is not.

You do not have to renew every year. The exemption stays in place as long as ownership and residency stay the same. If an assessor denies the application, the notice must give reasons, and the owner may appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review or the county commissioners. Maine Revenue Services Property Tax Bulletin No. 10 adds that denials of homestead, veteran and blind exemptions can go through the abatement process.

What changes on April 1, 2027?

The old section 683 states that its exemptions are discontinued for property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2027, and a new section, 36 M.R.S. §683-A, takes over from that date. Maine Revenue Services says the base homestead exemption stays at $25,000 of just value under the new section, and that veteran and blind exemptions are added to the same statute.

ItemBefore April 1, 2027From April 1, 2027
Base homestead exemptionUp to $25,000 of just value (§683)Up to $25,000 of just value (§683-A)
Veteran, age 62 or olderUp to $6,000 under the earlier veterans ruleUp to $6,000
Veteran with 100% service-connected ratingEarlier rules applyUp to $50,000
Legally blind permanent residentNot covered in the slidesUp to $5,000
Who must applyApply by April 1Current holders do not reapply unless they qualify for a higher amount

The Maine Revenue Services slides say applications for the higher amounts must be made to the local assessor before April 1, 2027. The 2027 figures also get multiplied by the local certified ratio. Both statutes tie the exemption to a permanent resident who has owned the homestead for the preceding 12 months.

How big is the program statewide?

Maine towns reported 325,426 homestead exemptions worth $7,410,258,960 in the 2025 Municipal Valuation Return, according to the Maine Revenue Services statistical summary.

MeasureFigureSource
Homestead exemptions, 2025 return325,426MRS 2025 valuation summary
Total value exempted$7,410,258,960MRS 2025 valuation summary
Total commitment, 2025$3,650,756,363MRS 2025 valuation summary
State reimbursement of lost taxes76%, towns absorb the restProperty tax task force coverage

Under current law the state reimburses 76% of the taxes lost to the exemption and municipalities absorb the rest. The task force recommended full reimbursement for any increase in the amount.

Does the homestead exemption affect selling a house in Maine?

Yes, in a quiet way: it affects who owes what in the year of the sale, and it can change what a buyer pays next year. Maine taxes what you own on April 1, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under 36 M.R.S. §502.

Closing usually involves a proration. Under §558 a buyer and seller may agree to split property tax pro rata over the municipality's fiscal year unless they agree on a different period. Since the bill already reflects your exemption for that year, the proration uses the lower number.

A buyer does not inherit your exemption. If the buyer will live in the house, they file their own application by April 1 and the town applies it to the next assessment. A buyer who cannot meet the twelve-month ownership test, or who plans to rent the house out, may not get the same bill you did.. Mention that to a buyer who is looking only at your old tax bill.

The state also charges a real estate transfer tax of $2.20 per $500 of value, split equally between buyer and seller under §4641-A. On a $300,000 sale that is $660 for each side.

What if you inherit a house that had a homestead exemption?

An inherited house that no one lives in will usually not keep the exemption, because the exemption rests on the owner using the home as a permanent residence. The FAQ says the break stays in effect only while ownership and residency are unchanged, and it does not spell out what to report after a death, so ask the assessor how the town handles it.

Heirs who plan to sell should look at the April 1 date. If the owner died after April 1 and the exemption was in place that day, the town has already set that year's bill. If the house sits vacant into the next tax year, expect a full bill with no exemption. Our Maine probate guide explains who has the authority to sell the property.

Does the state deferral program affect a sale?

The State Property Tax Deferral Program is the one that matters most at closing. To qualify, you must be 65 or older or unable to work due to permanent disability, with household income under $80,000 and liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with multiple owners). The state pays the tax, then places a lien on the home. Selling or transferring the home requires repayment of all deferred taxes, interest and costs. If you are leaving the program because of a sale, the payoff comes out of your proceeds.

Which sellers should check their homestead status before listing?

  • Owners who moved out and are renting the house. The home is no longer the permanent residence, so the exemption may have ended.
  • Owners who bought a second Maine home in the last year. You can have only one permanent residence.
  • Heirs holding a vacant house. Ownership has changed and residence has stopped.
  • Owners with a deferral lien. Expect a payoff figure from Maine Revenue Services at closing.

If any of these describes you and the house needs work you cannot afford before a sale, a direct sale to a cash buyer can simplify the tax side because there is no buyer financing or inspection renegotiation holding up the proration. That is the kind of situation Cash Home Buyers works with, and we do not promise a price until we see the property.

More questions about Maine Homestead Exemption

Is the Maine homestead exemption still $25,000?

Yes. Maine Revenue Services lists the exemption at up to $25,000 of just value as of April 1, 2026, and says the base stays at $25,000 under the new section starting April 1, 2027. The amount is multiplied by your town's certified ratio.

What is the deadline to apply?

April 1. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment, and the application goes to your municipal assessor.

Do I have to reapply every year?

No. The exemption stays in effect as long as ownership and residency do not change, according to the Maine Revenue Services FAQ.

Does the buyer get my homestead exemption when I sell?

No. The exemption belongs to the permanent resident who owns and lives in the home. A buyer who will live there files their own application by April 1.

Can I get the exemption on a camp or second home?

No. Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not qualify, and you can have only one permanent residence at a time.

What if the assessor denies my homestead application?

You may appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review or the county commissioners, and Property Tax Bulletin No. 10 notes that exemption denials can go through the abatement process.

Will the exemption stop in 2027?

The old section 683 is discontinued for tax years beginning April 1, 2027, but section 683-A takes over with a base exemption of up to $25,000, plus veteran and blind exemptions.

Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Maine estate tax exclusion amount (filing threshold) is $7,160,000 for 2026, $7,000,000 for 2025, $6,800,000 for 2024 and $6,410,000 for 2023. (Estate Tax FAQ | Maine Revenue Services; source)
  • Maine estate tax law places an automatic lien on real and tangible personal property of a decedent; release requires a Certificate of Discharge of Estate Tax Lien with Form 706ME or 700-SOV. (Estate Tax FAQ | Maine Revenue Services; source)
  • An estate in Maine probate may need to file Form 700-SOV or 706ME even if no tax is owed. (Estate Tax FAQ | Maine Revenue Services; source)
Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Maine have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

Maine has an estate tax, not an inheritance tax. The tax is figured on the whole estate before it is distributed, and heirs do not owe a separate tax on what they receive. One legal publisher's overview notes that the state does not impose an inheritance tax and that the estate tax fully replaced it for deaths after June 30, 1986.

For a family holding a house, the useful question is whether the estate is large enough to owe anything, and whether the paperwork for the lien release is in order. Some estates owe no tax and still have to file a short form so the house can be sold with a clean title.

The state's own definitions sit in 36 M.R.S. §4102. It treats the "adjusted federal gross estate" as the federal gross estate adjusted for Maine elective property, plus taxable gifts made in the year before death. A "resident" is a person domiciled in Maine at death, and a "nonresident" is someone domiciled elsewhere.

What is the Maine estate tax exclusion for 2026?

The 2026 Maine exclusion amount is $7,160,000. Maine Revenue Services publishes the amount for each year, and it has moved up over time.

Year of deathMaine exclusion amount
2023$6,410,000
2024$6,800,000
2025$7,000,000
2026$7,160,000

The federal exclusion for 2026 decedents is $15,000,000, according to the 2026 Form 706ME instructions. That gap is why a Maine estate can owe state tax even when no federal return is needed.

What are the Maine estate tax rates?

Tax applies only to the amount above the exclusion, in three steps. Table A in the 2026 Form 706ME instructions sets the rates.

Maine taxable amount (line 5)Tax
$7,160,000 or less$0
Over $7,160,000 up to $10,160,0008% of the amount over $7,160,000
Over $10,160,000 up to $13,160,000$240,000 plus 10% of the amount over $10,160,000
Over $13,160,000$540,000 plus 12% of the amount over $13,160,000

Interest and penalties are added to the tax owed. They are not deductions on the return.

Who has to file a Maine estate tax return?

A Maine return is required when the estate is above the threshold or when a federal estate tax return is required. The state lists the filing tests in its FAQ and the Form 706ME instructions.

  • A federal estate tax return is required.
  • The federal gross estate plus taxable gifts made within one year of death plus Maine elective property exceeds the threshold.
  • The Maine QTIP election on line 2 of Form 706ME is greater than zero.

Form 706ME applies to Maine residents, and to nonresidents who owned Maine real or tangible personal property at death. If a nonresident held Maine land through a trust, LLC or other pass-through entity, the state may still treat it as Maine property unless the entity had a valid business purpose, carried on a for-profit business and was acquired in a bona fide sale for full consideration. The personal representative files. If no one has been appointed, a person in possession of the estate's property is treated as the representative.

When is the return due, and can the estate get more time?

The return is due nine months after the date of death. Maine gives an automatic extension to file equal to any federal extension or six months, whichever is longer.

  • An extension to file does not extend the time to pay. Tax is due by the original date, and interest runs on unpaid tax.
  • A longer extension request must be in writing before the automatic six-month period ends, and the total generally cannot exceed eight months.
  • Estates largely made up of closely held business interests may request a payment extension under 36 M.R.S. §4109.
  • Penalties may be waived for reasonable cause. Interest waivers are rare.

Forms and payments go through the Maine Tax Portal, which does not require an account for estate tax filings. Form 706ME must be filed and paid electronically.

What is the Maine estate tax lien, and how does it affect a house sale?

Maine law places an automatic lien on a decedent's Maine real and tangible personal property at death. A buyer's title company will want to see a release before it insures a purchase, so the lien matters whenever an estate sells a house.

The representative requests the release with a Certificate of Discharge of Estate Tax Lien, plus either Form 706ME or Form 700-SOV (Statement of Value) and any required proof of value. The 706ME instructions cite 36 M.R.S. §4112 for the lien. The State Tax Assessor signs the certificate and mails it back, and the original is recorded with the county Registry of Deeds.

  • If no return is otherwise required, the estate files Form 700-SOV with the certificate to request the release.
  • Probate courts may require Form 700-SOV or 706ME even when no tax is owed.
  • If you lack the deed's book and page, the Registry of Deeds can help you find the reference.

Maine has 17 registry of deeds offices, one for each county and two for Aroostook, so the certificate must go to the office where the house sits.

How should heirs plan a sale around the lien and the tax?

Start the paperwork early, because the release is often the step that sets the closing date. Even a small estate with a single house benefits from a clear timeline.

  1. Confirm the date of death and value of all assets to see whether the estate is near the $7,160,000 threshold.
  2. Get a date-of-death appraisal of the house. The same value is generally used for the heirs' basis under IRS Publication 551.
  3. Prepare Form 700-SOV or Form 706ME with the Certificate of Discharge.
  4. Submit electronically through the Maine Tax Portal and wait for the signed certificate.
  5. Record the original at the registry of deeds in the county where the house is located.
  6. Schedule the closing after the release is recorded.

Maine also has other probate steps that run in parallel, covered in our Maine probate guide. A personal representative needs authority from the probate court to sign a deed, so line up those letters at the same time.

How do cash buyers handle an estate sale in Maine?

A cash buyer can close without bank underwriting, but the lien release and the estate's authority still decide the timeline. Heirs often come to us with a house that needs repairs, or one that sits empty while a family decides what to do. We buy as-is, and we work with your attorney or personal representative on the documents the title company needs.

This page is general information. For a specific estate, check with the personal representative's attorney or Maine Revenue Services before you sign a purchase contract.

More questions about Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax

What is the Maine estate tax threshold in 2026?

$7,160,000. Estates below that generally owe no Maine estate tax, though a form may still be needed to release the lien on real estate. The amount was $7,000,000 for 2025 and $6,800,000 for 2024.

Does Maine have an inheritance tax?

No. Maine uses an estate tax only, which is figured on the estate rather than on each heir's share. One published overview says the estate tax fully replaced the old inheritance tax for deaths after June 30, 1986.

Can heirs sell an inherited house in Maine before the estate tax is paid?

Usually the title company will require the Certificate of Discharge of Estate Tax Lien first. The lien attaches automatically at death, and the release is recorded at the county registry of deeds. Ask the personal representative's attorney how to time it.

What is Form 700-SOV?

It is the Statement of Value, which an estate files with a certificate request to release the lien when no estate tax return is otherwise required. The state says probate courts may ask for it even when no tax is owed.

When is the Maine estate tax return due?

Nine months after the date of death. Maine allows an automatic filing extension of six months or the federal extension, whichever is longer, but payment is still due by the original date.

Does a nonresident who owns a Maine house have to file?

Often yes. Form 706ME applies to nonresidents who owned Maine real or tangible personal property at death, and the estate's Maine property is entered on line 6a. The same lien release process applies.

What the official sources say

  • A 7-day written notice is available for grounds including 7 or more days of rent arrears, nuisance, substantial damage or unauthorized occupant. (14 M.R.S. §6002(2); source)
  • Paying full rent due before a 7-day arrears notice expires voids it; paying all arrears and fees before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy. (14 M.R.S. §6002; source)
  • The court issues the writ of possession 7 calendar days after judgment; a sheriff or constable may serve it. (14 M.R.S. §6005; source)
  • On sale of a rental, the person holding security deposits must account for and transfer them to the successor, and notify tenants by mail. (14 M.R.S. §6035; source)
  • When the landlord's interest ends by sale, the accounting and transfer must occur no later than the real estate closing, with written proof given to the buyer. (14 M.R.S. §6035; source)
Selling in Maine?

How does an eviction work in Maine?

A Maine landlord must give a written notice, then file a court case, then win a judgment, then wait for a writ of possession that a sheriff or constable serves. Maine calls the court case a forcible entry and detainer action, or FED, and 14 M.R.S. Chapter 709 governs it.

Each step has strict paperwork. A defective notice or a missed service step can reset the clock. If you own a rented house and are thinking about selling, it helps to know where the case stands, because the stage it has reached decides what a buyer can do.

This page uses the statutes and the Maine Judicial Branch's self-help guide for rent cases. It is general information, not legal advice.

Which notice does a Maine landlord have to serve first?

It depends on why the tenancy is ending. For a tenancy at will, 14 M.R.S. §6002 allows either side to end it with at least 30 days' written notice, and a 7-day notice for specific grounds.

NoticeWhen it is usedKey rule
30-day noticeEnding a tenancy at will without a stated faultMust tell the tenant of the right to contest in court; if rent is paid past the 30 days, the notice must expire on or after that date
7-day noticeRent 7 or more days in arrears, nuisance, substantial damage not repaired, unauthorized occupant, and certain violence-related groundsMust state the specific ground; a rent notice must state the amount owed and the cure statement

The statute lets a landlord combine a 30-day and a 7-day notice in one document. A clerical error in the arrears figure does not void the notice if it was unintentional and does not materially change its purpose. Starting January 1, 2024, landlords must also attach the judicial branch's form notice to termination notices, under 14 M.R.S. §6001.

How does a tenant stop an eviction for unpaid rent?

By paying. If the tenant pays the full rent due before a 7-day arrears notice expires, the notice is void. After it expires, paying all arrears, rent due and the filing and service fees before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy, and no writ may issue.

Payment or written assurance of payment through the general assistance program counts as cash for this purpose. That matters to a landlord planning a sale, because a nonpayment case can end suddenly when rent arrives.

A tenant can also raise the implied warranty of habitability in a nonpayment case. The landlord must have had actual or constructive notice of the problem and unreasonably failed to make repairs, and the tenant must not have caused it. If the court finds the unit unfit, the tenant owes only reduced fair rental value until repairs are made. The habitability duty itself appears in 14 M.R.S. §6021, which also covers heat and mold.

What are the court steps and costs for a rent case?

The Maine Judicial Branch lays out a seven-step path in its guide to evicting a tenant for not paying rent.

  1. Serve a 7-day notice to quit under §6002(1), with the information sheet (form CV-256).
  2. Prepare the complaint (CV-007), summons (CV-034, $5 each from the clerk) and the other required forms. List all tenants and add "and all other occupants" if others live there.
  3. Serve the papers through the county sheriff only after the notice period ends.
  4. File the notice to quit, the complaint, the summons with the return of service and the lease, with a $100 filing fee, before the hearing.
  5. Attend the hearing even if the tenant does not. Mediation is available at the court that day at no extra cost.
  6. If you win, you receive a judgment for possession and a writ of possession.
  7. If the tenant has not left, buy the writ from the clerk and hire a sheriff to serve it.

The guide says eviction does not collect back rent. That requires a separate case, often in Small Claims Court. Where a tenant cannot be served in hand after three good-faith attempts on three different days, 14 M.R.S. §6004 permits first-class mail plus leaving a copy at the tenant's last and usual residence, with an affidavit filed.

How long does a tenant have after the judgment?

The court issues the writ of possession seven calendar days after judgment is entered. After a sheriff or constable serves it, the tenant has 48 hours to leave, under 14 M.R.S. §6005.

A tenant who stays past 48 hours is treated as a trespasser, and the belongings are considered abandoned under §6013. No writ issues if the tenancy ended for rent arrears and the tenant paid the amount needed to reinstate.

An appeal can slow things. Under §6008, either party may appeal to Superior Court, and a defendant who appeals must pay the lesser of the unpaid current month's rent or the arrearage. The court can stay the writ on conditions such as continued rent payments. The deadline is the earlier of the writ's issuance or 30 days after judgment.

What happens to a tenant's belongings after an eviction?

The landlord must store them in a safe, dry, secured location and send written notice by first-class mail with proof of mailing. 14 M.R.S. §6013 sets out the timing.

  • The notice must include an itemized list of the items and containers.
  • The tenant has 7 days from the notice to claim the property.
  • If the tenant responds, the landlord must keep storing it for at least 14 days after sending the notice.
  • If the tenant claims the property within 7 days, release cannot be conditioned on fees or other amounts owed.
  • For unclaimed property, the landlord may sell it at a reasonable fair market price. Proceeds go first to back rent, damages and costs, and any balance goes to the Treasurer of State.

What can stop or delay an eviction?

Several defenses are written into the statute. Section 6001 creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation if, within 6 months before the action, the tenant asserted listed statutory rights, complained in good faith about code violations, made written repair requests or filed fair housing complaints. A writ cannot issue without rebuttal.

  • A tenant may raise a landlord's failure to provide a reasonable accommodation for a disability.
  • Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking cannot be evicted for those incidents.
  • A bona fide tenancy in a building with a pending foreclosure may be ended only under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009.
  • A new owner or assignee generally cannot bring the process against a tenant at will unless that tenant received proper notice under §6002.

What happens to a Maine rental when the owner sells?

Security deposits must be accounted for and transferred no later than the real estate closing. 14 M.R.S. §6035 says the holder of the deposits, including the landlord, agent or executor, must either transfer them to the successor with an accounting or return them to the tenants.

  • The seller mails each tenant notice of the transfer, the new owner's name and address, and a copy of the accounting.
  • At closing, the seller gives the buyer written proof of the accounting and transfer.
  • Once the holder complies, it is relieved of further liability for those funds, and the buyer takes the same duties as a landlord.
  • Under §6038, deposits must be kept in a bank account protected from the landlord's creditors, and a tenant can recover the greater of actual damages, $500 or one month's rent for a violation.

A tenant with a lease generally stays through a sale, because the buyer steps into the landlord's place. A buyer who wants the house empty has to wait for the lease to end or follow the notice rules above.

Should you evict first or sell the house with tenants in place?

It depends on timing and cost. An eviction can take weeks, adds filing and sheriff fees, and ends with a unit that may need work. Selling with tenants avoids that, but the buyer must accept the lease and the deposit transfer.

We buy Maine houses with tenants, unpaid rent or deferred repairs, as-is. A cash sale lets you hand off the property without waiting for a court date. If you are in the middle of a case, talk to a Maine attorney before you sign anything, and make sure the closing includes the deposit accounting that §6035 requires.

More questions about Maine Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Maine eviction take?

It depends on the notice period, the hearing date and whether the tenant appeals. The fixed pieces are a 7-day or 30-day notice, a writ issued 7 calendar days after judgment, and 48 hours for the tenant to leave once the writ is served.

How much notice does a Maine landlord have to give?

At least 30 days' written notice to end a tenancy at will, or a 7-day notice for grounds such as rent 7 or more days late, nuisance or substantial damage. A lease may add its own terms.

What is the filing fee for an eviction in Maine?

The Maine Judicial Branch's guide for rent cases lists a $100 filing fee, plus $5 for each summons from the clerk. Writ and sheriff service fees are separate.

Can I sell a house in Maine while the tenant is still there?

Yes. The tenant's lease generally continues with the new owner. At closing the seller must transfer or return security deposits, give the buyer written proof, and mail each tenant notice of the transfer.

Does eviction recover unpaid rent?

No. The court's guide says eviction does not collect back rent. That requires a separate case, often in Small Claims Court.

What if the tenant pays after getting a 7-day notice?

Paying all rent due before the notice expires voids it. Paying all arrears and filing and service fees after expiration but before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy, and no writ may issue.

How does probate work in Maine?

Maine probate is run by a county probate court, and the state has one in each of its 16 counties. The Maine Probate Court website says these courts handle the estates of deceased and missing persons, along with guardianships, trusts, name changes and adoptions. The first step is to file the appropriate forms in the county where the person lived at death.

The rules sit in the Maine Probate Code, Title 18-C of the Maine Revised Statutes. Most estates start with an application to the register of probate. Under 18-C M.R.S. §3-302 the register issues a written statement of informal probate once at least 120 hours have passed since the death, and the statement is conclusive until a formal testacy proceeding replaces it.

Filing can be done electronically. The probate court site lists an e-filing fee of $7 and notes that filing fees, surcharges, publication and certified mail may add to the cost. The courts cannot give legal advice, so many families hire an attorney for anything beyond a simple estate.

Who can be the personal representative of a Maine estate?

The person named in the will has first priority, and after that the order runs through the surviving spouse, other devisees, other heirs and then creditors. Section 3-203 sets the full list. Anyone who is 18 or older and has not been found unsuitable by the court in a formal proceeding is qualified.

  • A will-named representative comes first, including a person nominated by a power in the will.
  • A surviving spouse who is also a devisee comes next, then other devisees, then the surviving spouse alone, then other heirs.
  • Forty-five days after death, a creditor may seek appointment. Six months after death, if nothing has been opened, the State Tax Assessor may apply.
  • A person entitled to letters can nominate someone else, and anyone can renounce in writing filed with the court.

An objection to an appointment can be made only in a formal proceeding. If heirs cannot agree on who should serve, the house usually waits.

Can the personal representative sell the house without a court order?

Usually yes. Under §3-711 a personal representative has the same power over title as an absolute owner would have, held in trust for creditors and others interested in the estate, and may use it without notice, hearing or court order except as the section limits.

The main limit is notice. The representative may not sell or transfer any interest in estate real property without giving notice at least 10 days before the sale to anyone succeeding to an interest in it, unless the will authorizes a sale without notice. Section 3-715 separately lets the representative sell, mortgage or lease any real or personal property of the estate for cash or credit, at public or private sale, unless the will or a formal-proceeding order says otherwise.

A cash sale fits that framework easily. The representative signs a purchase agreement, gives the 10-day notice to the heirs, and closes with a deed signed as personal representative. Check the will first, because a will can restrict or widen the power.

Does Maine have a small estate shortcut, and does it cover real estate?

Maine has a small estate affidavit for personal property, but its title says it covers personal property only. Section 3-1201 allows a successor to collect personal property by affidavit when the entire estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $40,000 adjusted for inflation, 30 days have passed since the death, and no petition for a personal representative is pending anywhere.

The 2025 amendment requires each county probate court to publish the current inflation-adjusted figure on its website each year. Because the section deals with debts owed to the decedent and personal property held by others, it does not by itself move title to a house. If a house is part of the estate, plan on a regular appointment of a personal representative.

How long does a Maine estate stay open to creditors?

Claims are generally barred nine months after death, or earlier if notice is given. Section 3-803 says claims that arose before death are barred unless presented within the earlier of nine months after the death or the time allowed by the notice rules.

StepTime limitStatute
Informal probate by the registerAt least 120 hours after death18-C §3-302
Small estate affidavit30 days after death, estate under $40,000 (inflation adjusted)18-C §3-1201
Notice to creditors by publicationClaims within 4 months of first publication, two weekly notices18-C §3-801
Mailed notice to a known creditor4 months after publication or 60 days after mailing, whichever is later18-C §3-801
Claims arising before deathEarlier of 9 months or the notice period18-C §3-803
Ultimate limit to open probate3 years after death, with exceptions18-C §3-108

The representative publishes the notice once a week for two successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the person lived. Mortgages and other liens are not cut off by the claims bar, and the State can still pursue Medicaid reimbursement if it files within four months of notice.

What deadlines should heirs know before the house is sold?

A probate proceeding cannot generally be opened more than three years after the death. Section 3-108 sets that limit, with exceptions, including one that allows a late proceeding to confirm title if nothing happened in the first three years, though the representative then has limited authority and claims other than administration expenses cannot be presented.

A will contest against an informally probated will may be started within the later of 12 months from the informal probate or three years from the death.

What taxes and fees apply when an estate sells a Maine house?

Maine's real estate transfer tax applies to a sale, but a deed of distribution is exempt. The rate under 36 M.R.S. §4641-A is $2.20 per $500 of value, split equally between buyer and seller, so a $300,000 sale generates $660 from each side. Section 4641-C exempts deeds of distribution under Title 18-C, deeds between a parent and child with no consideration, and transfers by transfer-on-death deed.

A deed of distribution moves the house to an heir. A deed from the personal representative to an outside buyer is a sale. The exemption list does not mention personal representatives who sell to a buyer, so confirm with the registry of deeds or an attorney how the deed should be written.

Property tax follows the April 1 rule in 36 M.R.S. §502. The estate owes the bill for whatever was owned on April 1, and a buyer and seller can prorate over the municipality's fiscal year under §558. Our Maine property tax guide covers abatements and tax liens, and the homestead exemption page explains why a vacant inherited house may lose the exemption.

What problems do heirs run into with inherited Maine houses?

  • Heirs disagree on who should serve or whether to sell. Objections to an appointment require a formal proceeding.
  • The house has unpaid property tax. Maine uses tax lien mortgages, and if a taxpayer dies with a probated will, a probate judge may allow up to 60 more days to redeem after the will is allowed or disallowed (36 M.R.S. §943).
  • Repairs are deferred and the house sits vacant. A representative may retain assets pending distribution and may make repairs, but spending the estate's cash needs a plan.
  • Out-of-state heirs. Electronic filing helps, and a representative can sell without every heir being present, once the 10-day notice is given.

If the estate owns a house that needs work, a cash purchase lets the representative sell as-is, with no listing preparation. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on estate properties in Maine, and the representative still decides whether to accept. We do not quote a price before we review the house.

More questions about Maine Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do all Maine estates have to go through probate?

Not necessarily. Maine allows a small estate affidavit under 18-C M.R.S. §3-1201 when the whole estate is $40,000 or less (adjusted for inflation), but that section collects personal property and does not move title to a house. A house usually needs a personal representative.

Which court handles probate in Maine?

The county probate court where the person lived. Maine has a probate court in each of its 16 counties, and filings can be made electronically.

Can a personal representative sell a house in Maine without court approval?

Usually yes. Under §3-711 the representative has the same power over title as an absolute owner, but must give at least 10 days' notice to people succeeding to an interest unless the will waives it.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a Maine estate?

Claims that arose before death are barred nine months after death, or earlier if the notice to creditors period ends first. Published notice gives creditors 4 months from first publication.

Is there a transfer tax when an estate sells a house in Maine?

A sale is subject to the transfer tax of $2.20 per $500 of value, split between buyer and seller. Deeds of distribution under Title 18-C are exempt.

How long can I wait to open probate in Maine?

Generally three years after death, with limited exceptions listed in §3-108. Waiting that long limits what the representative can do.

Who has priority to serve as personal representative?

The person named in the will, then the surviving spouse who is a devisee, other devisees, the surviving spouse, other heirs, and later creditors and the State Tax Assessor under §3-203.

What the official sources say

  • For sales on or after January 1, 2021, withholding applies only when consideration is $100,000 or more. (Real Estate Withholding (REW) | Maine Revenue Services; source)
  • The buyer withholds and remits using Form REW-1. (Real Estate Withholding (REW) | Maine Revenue Services; source)

Does Maine have a separate capital gains tax on a house sale?

No. Maine does not publish a separate capital gains rate for home sales. Under 36 M.R.S. §5121, a resident's Maine taxable income starts with federal adjusted gross income, so a taxable gain on your house is carried into the Maine return and taxed on the regular graduated schedule.

That means two questions decide what you owe on a Maine house sale. First, how much of the gain does the federal home sale exclusion remove? Second, where does what is left land on the Maine rate schedule for your filing status?

Both answers depend on facts the sale price alone does not show: how long you lived in the house, what you paid for it, what you spent on improvements, and whether you live in Maine now. This page walks through each piece so you can estimate the bill before you sign anything.

How much of the gain can a Maine homeowner exclude?

Most owners who lived in the house can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. The IRS describes this in Topic 701, and because the excluded gain never reaches federal adjusted gross income, it does not reach the Maine return either.

TestWhat the IRS says
OwnershipYou or your spouse owned the home at least 24 months of the 5 years before the sale
Use as main homeYou and your spouse each used it as a main residence at least 24 months of those 5 years
Exclusion limitUp to $250,000, or $500,000 if filing jointly
FrequencyGenerally not available if you excluded gain on another home sale within the 2 years before this sale
ReportingA Form 1099-S must be reported even if all the gain is excludable; Form 8949 and Schedule D are used if some gain is not excludable

The two-year ownership and use periods can fall in different stretches, as long as both are met inside the five-year window that ends on the sale date. Partial exclusions and depreciation are handled in IRS Publication 523, which Topic 701 points to.

What are Maine's income tax rates on the gain you cannot exclude?

For 2026 Maine uses three brackets: 5.8 percent, 6.75 percent and 7.15 percent. The thresholds below come from the 2026 Maine Revenue Services rate schedule.

Filing status5.8% applies below6.75% bracket7.15% applies at or above
Single or married filing separately$27,400$27,400 to $64,850$64,850
Head of household$41,100$41,100 to $97,300$97,300
Married filing jointly$54,850$54,850 to $129,750$129,750

Starting with tax years beginning in 2026, a 2 percent surcharge applies to Maine taxable income above $1,000,000 for a single filer, $750,000 for married filing separately, and $1,500,000 for married filing jointly or head of household. A large gain from a high-value house or a multi-parcel sale can reach that level.

The same schedule lists a 2026 standard deduction of $15,700 for a single filer and $31,400 for a joint return, plus a $5,300 personal exemption per taxpayer.

What federal rate applies to a taxable house gain?

A house you owned for more than one year produces a long-term gain, taxed federally at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on income. The IRS explains the holding period and rates in Topic 409.

  • For taxable years beginning in 2025, the 0 percent rate applies at or below $48,350 (single), $96,700 (married filing jointly) or $64,750 (head of household).
  • The 15 percent rate runs up to $533,400 (single), $600,050 (married filing jointly) or $566,700 (head of household).
  • Above those amounts the rate is 20 percent.
  • Gain on a house held one year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.
  • The portion of gain from real property that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taxed at a maximum 25 percent.

The Maine bill is added on top of the federal one. Someone with a $90,000 taxable gain owes Maine tax at the Maine brackets above, no matter which federal rate applies.

What happens if you live outside Maine and sell a Maine house?

The buyer or closing agent must withhold 2.5 percent of the sale price when the seller is a nonresident and the price is $100,000 or more. Maine Revenue Services' real estate withholding FAQ says this applies to nonresident individuals, estates and businesses.

  • The withholding is an estimated payment toward Maine tax on the gain. It is not the final tax.
  • With several owners, the buyer withholds 2.5 percent of each nonresident seller's share.
  • The buyer or escrow person files Form REW-1 and pays within 30 days of closing.
  • A Maine resident who does not hand over a signed residency affidavit (Form REW-2 or REW-3) is treated as a nonresident for this purpose.
  • A partnership counts as a Maine resident if at least 75 percent of its ownership is held by Maine residents on the transfer date.

Heirs who live out of state and inherit a Maine house are often surprised here. An estate selling Maine property is within the withholding rule too, so the closing agent will ask for a residency affidavit or an exemption certificate.

How can a seller reduce or avoid the 2.5 percent withholding?

File Form REW-5 with Maine Revenue Services before closing. The state says a seller cannot obtain an exemption or reduction after closing, and it asks for at least 5 business days to respond.

  • A full exemption may be available if there is no gain, or if a federal exclusion of gain on a principal residence applies. The state's page does not list a principal residence as a standalone exemption, so the request goes through REW-5.
  • A reduction is possible when your maximum Maine tax on the gain is below 2.5 percent of the sale price. The state calculates it as 7.15 percent of the gain, plus 2 percent of the gain above $1,000,000 (single), $1,500,000 (head of household or married filing jointly) or $750,000 (married filing separately) for tax year 2026.
  • Estates and trusts use 7.15 percent plus 2 percent of gain above $1,000,000. Corporations use 8.93 percent.
  • A like-kind exchange under IRC §1031 still triggers withholding, but you can ask for an exemption with REW-5 and a copy of the exchange contract.
  • Installment sales may qualify for a reduction based on first-year gain.

Consideration under $100,000 avoids withholding, but the state notes that federally taxable gains are still taxable in Maine regardless of the amount. A nonresident seller should expect to file a Maine income tax return for the year of the sale to claim any refund of excess withholding. Refund claims are generally due within three years of the return due date or three years from payment, whichever is later.

How does an inherited house change the numbers?

An heir's starting point is usually the house's value on the date of death, not what the owner paid. IRS Publication 551 lists fair market value at death, the alternate valuation date if the estate elects it, and special-use valuation for qualifying farm or business property.

If the estate had to file a federal Form 706, beneficiaries usually receive a Schedule A (Form 8971), and certain beneficiaries must use the reported value as their basis. One exception: if you or your spouse gave the property to the decedent within one year before death, your basis is the decedent's adjusted basis rather than the date-of-death value.

For a Maine family, this often means a house inherited and sold within a year or two shows little or no gain. The estate-side issues, including Maine's own estate tax lien, are covered on ourx. Basis is generally what you paid, plus improvements that add value, minus allowable depreciation, as the IRS describes in Topic 703.

How does a cash sale fit with Maine tax planning?

A cash sale does not change the tax rules, but it makes the closing date predictable, which helps you plan. You know when the gain is realized, when any withholding is due, and which tax year it belongs to. If you are a nonresident, you can also raise the REW-5 request early, because a seller cannot get an exemption or reduction after closing.

Sellers in Maine often come to us because of an inherited house, a rental with tenants or deferred repairs. Each of those has its own tax angle: basis for heirs, depreciation for landlords, and withholding for owners who moved away. Talk to a licensed tax professional about your own numbers. We can give you a straightforward offer and let your closing agent and accountant handle the filings.

More questions about Maine Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Maine tax the profit when I sell my house?

Yes, if the gain is taxable. A resident's Maine income starts from federal adjusted gross income, so any gain not excluded under the federal home sale rules is taxed at Maine's graduated rates. For 2026 those rates are 5.8, 6.75 and 7.15 percent.

How much of my gain can I exclude when selling my Maine home?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the house as your main home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years. You generally cannot use it if you excluded gain on another home within the prior 2 years.

What is Maine real estate withholding?

It is a 2.5 percent withholding on the sale price when a nonresident sells Maine property for $100,000 or more. The buyer or closing agent files Form REW-1 and pays within 30 days of closing. It is only an estimate of the seller's Maine tax.

Can I get the withholding waived?

Possibly. File Form REW-5 with Maine Revenue Services before closing. Exemptions or reductions are available in cases such as no gain, a federal principal residence exclusion, or when your maximum Maine tax is below 2.5 percent of the price. It cannot be requested after closing.

Do heirs owe Maine tax on an inherited house they sell?

Only on gain above their basis. Inherited property generally takes its fair market value at the date of death as basis, so a sale soon after inheritance often shows little gain. A nonresident heir may still face withholding at closing.

Is there a surcharge on large gains in Maine?

Yes, for tax years beginning in 2026. A 2 percent surcharge applies to Maine taxable income above $1,000,000 for single filers, $750,000 for married filing separately, and $1,500,000 for joint filers and heads of household.

Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax: Rates, Exemptions and Who Pays

Cash Home Buyers in Maine

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The tax is imposed one-half on the grantor and one-half on the grantee. (36 M.R.S. §4641-A; source)
  • Deeds of distribution under Title 18-B or 18-C, tax deeds, and deeds under the US Bankruptcy Code are exempt. (36 M.R.S. §4641-C(5), (11), (14); source)
  • Deeds to purchasers receiving Maine State Housing Authority first-time home-buyer mortgage assistance are exempt, for both buyer and seller. (36 M.R.S. §4641-C(22); source)
Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How much is the Maine real estate transfer tax?

Maine's transfer tax is $2.20 for each $500, or fractional part of $500, of the property's value. For transfers on or after November 1, 2025, value above $1 million carries an extra $3.80 per $500, which makes the rate on that top slice $6.00 per $500. The rate is set in 36 M.R.S. section 4641-A.

Because the tax counts every partial $500 as a full unit, a sale at $200,001 is taxed as though it were $200,500. The registry rounds up, and so should your estimate.

The table below uses the rate and the state's own tax chart and bulletin. Each figure is the total, and the seller and buyer each owe half.

Sale priceTotal taxSeller's halfBuyer's half
$100,000$440.00$220.00$220.00
$250,000$1,100.00$550.00$550.00
$500,000$2,200.00$1,100.00$1,100.00
$815,500$3,588.20$1,794.10$1,794.10
$1,500,000$10,400.00$5,200.00$5,200.00

The first four rows come from the Maine Revenue Services tax chart, and the last is the worked example in its Property Tax Bulletin 31. The chart is built for sales on or after November 1, 2025.

Who pays the Maine transfer tax, the seller or the buyer?

The seller (the grantor) pays half and the buyer (the grantee) pays half. Section 4641-A states the split, and the register of deeds collects both halves when the deed is offered for recording.

On a $300,000 sale, for example, 600 units of $500 at $2.20 gives $1,320 in total, so each side owes $660. That is a real line on the closing statement, and it is easy to miss when you are comparing offers. A seller who is told a cash buyer covers all closing costs should ask in writing whether that includes the seller's half of the transfer tax.

If you disagree with the amount the register computes, section 4641-B lets a person ask the State Tax Assessor to determine the correct amount so the deed can still be recorded.

What value is the tax based on?

The tax is based on the value stated on the transfer tax declaration, which is normally the actual price paid. Maine Revenue Services Bulletin 31 explains that consideration usually means money but can also include other property or the assumption of an existing mortgage.

  • For an arm's-length sale, the value is the consideration.
  • For a gift, a nominal-price transfer or a deal where the consideration cannot be determined, the value is fair market value.
  • The bulletin treats the adjusted assessed value (the municipal assessed value divided by the municipality's certified ratio) as fair market value unless the local assessor says otherwise.
  • "Nominal" means less than 20 percent of the adjusted assessed value.

Preparers filing declarations online have to enter the property's adjusted assessed value, which they can get from the municipal assessor. That figure is also why selling a house to a relative for $1 does not produce a $1 tax base: the declaration will be compared with what the town says the house is worth.

Which sales and transfers are exempt?

Maine exempts a long list of deeds, and the ones that matter to most home sellers involve family, death, divorce, bankruptcy and certain lenders. Section 4641-C contains the full numbered list. The most relevant:

  • Deeds between spouses, parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild with no actual consideration, and deeds between spouses in divorce proceedings
  • Deeds of distribution under Title 18-B or Title 18-C, which covers an estate passing property to heirs
  • Transfers by transfer on death deed
  • Tax deeds and deeds given under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code
  • Corrective deeds that change nothing about price or ownership
  • Mortgage deeds, discharges and partial releases
  • Deeds to the U.S., the State or their agencies and subdivisions
  • Deeds to buyers receiving Maine State Housing Authority first-time homebuyer mortgage assistance, exempt for both buyer and seller
  • Conveyances of a mobile home park to a majority of its residents or a residents' association under Title 10, section 9094-A

An exemption does not apply itself. The bulletin says it has to be claimed and specifically identified on the declaration, and section 4641-D requires the declaration to state the reason when a transfer is exempt.

How does the tax work in a foreclosure or deed in lieu?

Maine treats the common distressed-sale deeds differently, and the bulletin spells out each one. If you are behind on a mortgage, this is where the rules pay off.

SituationWho owes tax
Deed in lieu of foreclosureThe mortgagor (owner) is exempt. The mortgagee pays half, based on the property's value.
Foreclosure auction sold to a third partyThe buyer pays half on the sale price. The seller pays half but only on any profit, so no profit means no seller tax.
Foreclosing lender is the high bidderThe lender is treated as both buyer and seller and pays the full tax on the sale price.
Mortgage deedNo tax for either party.

The practical point is that giving a lender a deed in lieu costs the owner no transfer tax, while a normal sale before foreclosure does carry the seller's half. A seller weighing the two should compare the seller's half of the tax against the other costs of each path.

Does the tax apply when an LLC or other entity changes hands?

Yes. Section 4641-A also taxes the transfer or acquisition of a controlling interest in an entity that holds Maine real estate, when it happens within any 12-month period. The same rates apply to the value of the property, and the transferor and transferee each pay half.

Controlling-interest transfers are reported to the register of deeds, not recorded as deeds. If the transfer is not reported and the tax paid within 30 days of completion, both parties become jointly and severally liable for the whole amount. That matters to an owner who holds a rental house in an LLC and plans to sell the company instead of the deed. A transfer that would have been exempt as a deed is also exempt as a controlling-interest transfer.

Maine Revenue Services publishes a separate controlling interest declaration form for these deals.

How and when is the tax collected?

The register of deeds in the county where the property sits computes the tax and collects it at the moment the deed is offered for recording. Nothing is billed afterward, and the declaration that comes with the deed serves as the return. The register gets the money before the deed is accepted.

Under the bulletin, the register keeps 9.2 percent of the tax and sends 90.8 percent to Maine Revenue Services every month, and the declarations go to the State within 40 days of recording. Under section 4641-B, registers remit by the 10th of each month for the prior month, and the statute sets the State's share at 90.8 percent for fiscal years 2025-26 and 2026-27.

For a seller the key date is the closing date. Plan for the registry to need the declaration, the signed deed and payment on that day. Our Maine deed recording guide covers the fees and formatting that go with it.

What should a Maine seller do before closing?

  1. Estimate the tax with the state's tax chart or estimate calculator, which Maine Revenue Services links from its transfer tax page.
  2. Ask who is paying the seller's half, and get the answer on the contract.
  3. Check whether your deed qualifies for an exemption and tell the closing agent so it goes on the declaration.
  4. If the buyer uses a Maine State Housing Authority first-time buyer loan, ask the closer to confirm the exemption for both sides.
  5. If the property is in an entity, ask a lawyer whether a controlling-interest transfer is involved.

This page is general information, not tax or legal advice. Maine Revenue Services can answer calculation questions at prop.tax@maine.gov, and the county registry can confirm what it will accept on closing day.

More questions about Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax

What is the Maine real estate transfer tax rate?

The rate is $2.20 for each $500 or fractional part of $500 of value. For transfers on or after November 1, 2025, value above $1 million adds $3.80 per $500, so that slice is taxed at $6.00 per $500.

Does the seller pay the transfer tax in Maine?

The seller pays half and the buyer pays half. The register of deeds collects both shares when the deed is recorded, so the seller's half normally comes out of the proceeds at closing unless the contract says otherwise.

How much is the transfer tax on a $400,000 house in Maine?

The total is $1,760, which is 800 units of $500 at $2.20, so each side owes $880. That figure is our arithmetic from the statutory rate, and the registry's own computation controls at closing.

Is there a Maine transfer tax on an inherited house?

A deed of distribution from an estate under Title 18-B or 18-C is exempt. A sale by the heirs afterward is a normal sale and carries the tax, split between seller and buyer.

Is a deed in lieu of foreclosure subject to Maine transfer tax?

The owner giving the deed is exempt. The lender pays half of the tax based on the property's value, according to Maine Revenue Services Bulletin 31.

Do first-time buyers pay the Maine transfer tax?

Buyers using a Maine State Housing Authority first-time homebuyer mortgage program are exempt, and so is the seller on that deed. The exemption has to be claimed on the declaration.

What the official sources say

  • Registry of deeds recording fee for an instrument without a specific fee is $35 (or $25 if recorded at the request of the State or a municipality). (33 M.R.S. §751; source)
  • Plans are $45 to record; fees are payable when the instrument is offered for record. (33 M.R.S. §751; source)
